title: How to Detect Hallucinations in AI Agents in Production
summary: Detect hallucinations in AI agents by checking claims against tool results in the trace: four kinds, which method catches each, and a tested Laminar Signal.
body_markdown:
Detecting hallucinations in an AI agent means checking its claims against the evidence available when it made them. A flight-rebooking agent calls get_fare_rules


, the call times out, and the agent tells the customer the change fee is $75. Without another source for that amount, the fee is unsupported. A plausible reply and a completed run do not establish that the answer is grounded.


In Laminar's[taxonomy of agent failures](https://laminar.sh/blog/taxonomy-of-agent-failures) , hallucination accounted for 26% of sampled production failures. About 86% of agents represented in that analysis hallucinated at least once, and only 3% of fabrications were marked as recovered. These are findings from a project-balanced, LLM-labeled failure sample, not estimates for all production agents or their traffic.


This guide maps four kinds of hallucination to detection methods, then builds a Laminar workflow tested on ten scripted traces. The goal is to find unsupported claims automatically while keeping enough evidence for a reviewer to assess each finding.


*Illustrative, scripted example: the timed-out fare-rules call leaves the $75 fee unsupported; the flight-search result contradicts the claim that seats are available. The timeout alone does not prove the fee is false.*


## Four kinds of agent hallucination#


An agent makes factual claims and reports actions. Both need evidence, but the checks differ.


Kind Rebooking example Evidence to inspect Share of sampled failures


Fabricated fact Quotes a $75 change fee Fare-rules call timed out; no other source supplies the fee 13.2%


Contradicts a tool result Says SK 212 has seats Search returned seats_available: 0


6.8%


Unsupported success claim Says rebooking and email succeeded Rebooking failed; no email call appears 5.5%


Fake or denied tool call Claims a loyalty lookup No corresponding tool call appears 1.0%


The shares come from the taxonomy's equal-per-project failure sample. Its model-based labels can contain false positives or skews, and the analysis is correlational.


A fabricated fact lacks support; a contradiction has evidence saying the opposite. An unsupported success claim concerns an action's outcome. A fake or denied tool call concerns what the agent invoked or could invoke. One sentence can fit multiple kinds.


Missing evidence needs careful interpretation. An absent call is meaningful only if you captured the relevant execution path. A timeout can leave an action's outcome unknown. Distinguish “the trace does not support success” from “the external system definitely did nothing.”


## Choose a hallucination detector by the evidence it reads#


Two choices determine coverage: what evidence the detector receives, and which replies it evaluates. Reading a complete conversation does not necessarily mean checking every intermediate response.


Method Evidence supplied Useful for Main limit


Final-answer judge Question and last reply Internal inconsistencies or suspicious claims Cannot establish agreement with unseen tool results


Groundedness check Response and supplied context Claims unsupported by that context Coverage depends on what the context contains


Reference-answer check Response and expected answer Known-answer cases Many production requests have no reference answer


Deterministic check Named spans, statuses, fields or text Explicit action contracts Brittle matching and incomplete execution evidence


Whole-trace check Calls, results, errors and conversation Cross-step claims and action reporting Still needs complete evidence and explicit reply coverage


A groundedness check can assess action claims if you supply the execution evidence as context. Conversely, a whole-trace judge can miss a mid-run hallucination if its target is only the final reply. The method's name does not establish its coverage.


Arize Phoenix's Hallucination evaluator documentation specifies conversation input that can include tool calls, tool results and retrieved content, with trace- or session-level application. Its target output is the assistant's latest response. Phoenix's Faithfulness evaluator instead grounds a response in one retrieved-context block.


Datadog LLM Observability's managed Hallucination evaluation checks LLM-span output against annotated RAG query and context. Its documentation says it skips evaluation when required inputs are empty, detects contradictions and optionally includes unsupported claims. Datadog also documents custom trace-scoped judges that receive every span.


Braintrust's autoevals Factuality template requires an expected answer. Separately, its online scoring documentation supports custom trace-scoped scorers that can inspect nested spans. Reference-based scoring is therefore one option within the product, not its production-detection boundary.


For an agent, provide execution evidence and explicitly include intermediate user-facing replies. Add deterministic checks for action contracts you can define precisely. For a single-response retrieval workflow, a supplied-context check may be sufficient; a whole trace is not inherently necessary.


### Include claims made before the final answer#


In one scripted trace, fare rules said refundable: false


. The agent then told the customer the fare was refundable. Rebooking succeeded, and the final reply was accurate. Checking only that last reply would leave the earlier refund claim unexamined.


Evaluate claims against evidence available at the time. A later correction may show recovery, but it does not erase what the customer was previously told.


### Reserve literal rules for literal contracts#


A rule that flags every number absent from tool output will reject valid calculations. In another test trace, the agent added a $75 fee to a $40 fare difference and quoted $115. The total appeared in neither tool result, but followed from both. The tested model-based check left that control unflagged; this does not establish general arithmetic reliability.


## Step 1: Capture the evidence in your trace#


Record tool arguments, results and failures alongside the agent's user-facing replies. Check what your framework integration captures rather than assuming every dispatch is visible. Laminar's[integrations](https://laminar.sh/docs/integrations) instrument many frameworks automatically; for manually dispatched tools, use the TOOL


[span type](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/structure/span-types) :


```text
from   lmnr   import   Laminar  ,   observe


Laminar  .  initialize  (  )


@observe  (  name  =  "get_fare_rules"  ,   span_type  =  "TOOL"  )
def     get_fare_rules  (  fare_class  :     str  )     -  >     dict  :
return   fares_api  .  get_rules  (  fare_class  )


```


The decorator records arguments and return values. In our SDK test, raising TimeoutError


produced a span with type TOOL


, status error


and input {"fare_class": "Basic"}


. Name spans consistently with the tools exposed to the model.


To assess denied-tool claims, also capture which tools were available. The scripted traces included definitions on LLM spans and a tool list in the system prompt. When the detector flagged “I'm not able to send emails from this chat,” it cited that prompt.


Tool availability alone does not establish authorization for every request. Your production checks should distinguish an unavailable tool from an action prohibited by permissions or policy.


## Step 2: Define a hallucination Signal#


In Laminar, you can define a[Signal](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/introduction) with an instruction and a JSON event schema. The Signals agent reads the trace and returns findings with evidence links, or no event when it finds no match. These are model judgments, not guarantees.


The following instruction and schema were tested through the project API. You can enter them in the Create Signal drawer or use the documented[Signals CLI](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/cli) :


```text
lmnr-cli signal create   "Hallucinated claims"     \
--prompt     "Find claims in the agent's replies to the user that the trace does not support. Report a fact that no tool result, retrieved document or user message provides (fabricated_fact); a statement that contradicts a tool result (contradicts_tool_result); a claim that an action succeeded when no successful tool call shows it (unsupported_success_claim); and a claim to have called a tool that was never called, or a claim that an available tool does not exist (fake_tool_call). Do not report statements the agent marks as uncertain, or tone and policy wording."     \
--schema     '{"properties":{
"kind":{"type":"string","enum":["fabricated_fact","contradicts_tool_result","unsupported_success_claim","fake_tool_call"],"description":"Which kind of unsupported claim this is"},
"claim":{"type":"string","description":"The agent claim, quoted from its reply"},
"evidence":{"type":"string","description":"The tool result or error that contradicts or fails to support the claim, or the tool call that never happened"}}}'


```


“The agent's replies” asks for coverage beyond the final answer. The kind


enum supports SQL grouping and alert filters. Quoted claims and evidence descriptions make findings easier to review; evidence text linked to cited spans in most test events.


The instruction deliberately excludes statements marked uncertain and tone or policy wording. It therefore does not cover every misleading utterance. Review those exclusions against your agent's behavior before adopting them.


## Step 3: Backfill and inspect known cases#


Before relying on alerts, run the detector on traces with reviewed labels. In the Signal's Overview tab, you can backfill a time range, filtered traces or selected trace IDs, as described in the[Signals quickstart](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/quickstart) .


The walkthrough test used ten scripted flight-rebooking traces with hand-written tool results and replies, recorded with the Laminar Python SDK. Seven contained hallucinations; three were controls. The same ten traces were backfilled twice.


This was a self-hosted local enterprise build using Gemini 3 Flash (preview) through an[LLM profile](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/llm-profiles) . Laminar Cloud uses flow-1 for Signals. These results do not measure Cloud performance.


Scripted case Expected label Flagged across two runs


Quotes a fee after fare-rules timeout fabricated_fact 2 of 2


Says a full flight has seats contradicts_tool_result 2 of 2


Says failed rebooking and missing email succeeded unsupported_success_claim 2 of 2


Claims loyalty lookup and Gold status fake_tool_call, with overlapping fabrication 2 of 2


Denies an available email tool fake_tool_call 2 of 2


Makes a false mid-run refund claim contradicts_tool_result 2 of 2


Claims a search that never ran fake_tool_call 2 of 2


Admits it cannot quote after timeout no event 0 of 2


Reports successful rebooking and email no event 0 of 2


Calculates $115 from two returned amounts no event 0 of 2


All seven positive traces were flagged in both runs, with no events on the three controls. An earlier run on seven traces with a draft schema produced the same detections. This demonstrates behavior on these seeded cases, not production precision, recall, latency or cost.


Labels were less stable than detection. Across all three runs containing the loyalty case, it received fabricated_fact


twice and fake_tool_call


once. Every flagged trace produced one event in this test, including the reply containing both failed-rebooking and missing-email claims. That is an observation, not a documented one-event-per-trace rule or a claim count.


The fee, seat, refund and false-success cases received critical severity whenever tested. The denied-email and claimed-search cases received warning. The loyalty case varied between critical and warning. Do not treat either kind or severity as a fixed impact classification.


Next, review representative production traces, including retries, incomplete traces and legitimate refusals. When you discard a finding with a reason, Laminar adds that reason to the instruction for future runs. Recheck previously labeled cases after changing instructions.


## Step 4: Query findings and action-check candidates#


In Laminar's[SQL editor](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/sql-editor) , you can query signal_events


; schema fields live in the JSON payload


. This query groups the week's recorded findings:


```text
SELECT
simpleJSONExtractString  (  payload  ,     'kind'  )     AS   kind  ,
count  (  )     AS   events  ,
uniq  (  trace_id  )     AS   traces
FROM   signal_events
WHERE   signal_name   =     'Hallucinated claims'
AND     timestamp     >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     7     DAY
GROUP     BY   kind
ORDER     BY   events   DESC


```


These are event and trace counts, not hallucination rates. A rate also needs the number of eligible traces actually checked, accounting for filters and sampling. Overlapping labels should not be treated as mutually exclusive production categories.


You can also query action-check candidates directly. This example assumes the rebooking_agent


span's output contains the user-facing reply:


```text
SELECT   trace_id  ,   output
FROM   spans
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     1     DAY
AND   name   =     'rebooking_agent'
AND     (  output   ILIKE     '%emailed%'     OR   output   ILIKE     '%inbox%'  )
AND   trace_id   NOT     IN     (
SELECT   trace_id
FROM   spans
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     1     DAY
AND   span_type   =     'TOOL'
AND   name   =     'send_confirmation_email'
AND     status     =     'success'
)


```


In the test project, this returned only the failed-rebooking trace. It excluded the two traces with successful email calls.


The query is a lexical heuristic. It can match “I haven't emailed” and miss paraphrases. It checks span status, not email delivery, and its time window can exclude earlier calls. The test encoded tool failures as error spans; your tool may return a business failure without raising an exception. Review output semantics, retries and trace completeness before treating a match as proof of an unperformed action.


## Step 5: Route findings by operational impact#


After deployment, the check runs on eligible completed traces. It can help you discover recurring failures, but it does not prevent the current reply from reaching the user.


Through[Signal alerts](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/alerts) , you can filter findings by schema fields and severity. Creating a Signal also creates a New event alert scoped to critical severity, with similar-event suppression enabled, plus a New cluster alert. The warning-level findings in this test would not satisfy the default critical-only event filter.


Choose routing by consequence. Unsupported booking confirmations may need immediate investigation. A fake lookup can also matter if it affects authorization or a customer decision, so do not automatically relegate that category to a digest. Review all severity levels during calibration before deciding which deserve an interruption. To page on one kind, add an output schema filter on kind


and include Warning in the alert's severity set.


Similar-event suppression notifies on the first event in a semantically similar group. It does not guarantee one notification per underlying outage. You can inspect recurring patterns through[clusters](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/clusters) , while retaining individual findings for review. Keep alert volume separate from incident volume and from the number of affected traces.


## FAQ#


### Does an unsupported claim have to be false?#


No. A claim can be true without support in the trace. This instruction applies a strict trace-grounding rule; it cannot establish world truth. Decide which business claims require recorded provenance. If your agent may use general knowledge, define and test appropriate exclusions rather than labeling every unsourced sentence false.


### What should happen after a reviewer confirms a hallucination?#


Keep the trace, disputed claim, evidence and reviewed label as a regression case. Test both the agent fix and the detector: correcting the agent's behavior and recognizing a bad response are separate tasks. Include a nearby valid case to catch overcorrection. The guide to[evaluating AI agents](https://laminar.sh/article/how-to-evaluate-ai-agents) covers the broader evaluation workflow.


### How does this differ from the default Issues Signal?#


New projects include an Issues Signal that looks broadly for agent errors and records a free-text description


. A dedicated hallucination detector adds structured categories for queries and routing. You do not necessarily need both running over identical traffic. If both flag one trace, avoid counting their findings as two independent incidents.


### How should I control detection cost at scale?#


Set coverage using failure impact, traffic volume and measured token consumption. Per-user sampling controls are documented from 5% to 95%; a sample can miss rare but consequential failures. Each Signal run is billed by the tokens its agent uses, not merely the trace's input length. Review[usage limits](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/usage-limits) , and measure detection delay alongside cost before setting operational expectations.


### Why might short conversations never be checked?#


The default Signal filter requires more than 1,000 total tokens. A short exchange containing one tool call and a fabricated fee can fall below that threshold. Lower or remove the total-token filter when those conversations matter, and inspect sampling separately. No event can mean no match, but it can also mean the trace was never analyzed.
